cards.title: Map decisions with Responsibility Charting (R, A-V, S, I)
cards.summary: Build a decisions-by-actors grid assigning Responsibility, Approval/veto, Support or Inform to end ownership ambiguity.
cards.use_when: When launches stall because nobody knows who can approve, veto, fund or needs notifying — pricing changes, promotions, product selection, site changes.

cards.title: Use Force Field Analysis to unblock a stalled situation
cards.summary: Move a team from current to desired state by weighing driving versus restraining forces and acting on the ones you control.
cards.use_when: When a store initiative (site speed migration, returns process fix, listing quality standard) keeps stalling despite agreement that it matters.

cards.title: Run a role negotiation contract when resistance is power-based
cards.summary: When people resist change because it threatens their influence, negotiate explicit behavior contracts instead of discussing feelings.
cards.use_when: When a functional owner (e.g., a category lead or channel owner) blocks a workflow change that would reduce their control.

cards.title: Choose the team type that matches the work
cards.summary: Match team structure — functional, project, cross-functional, self-managing, problem-solving, quality circle, task force — to the duration and authority the work needs.
cards.use_when: Setting up a squad for a defined need: a site redesign, a marketplace launch, a continuous improvement routine, or ongoing category management.

cards.title: Build the twelve conditions of effective teams into how you run meetings
cards.summary: Audit your team's operating habits against the source's effective-team characteristics and fix the weakest ones.
cards.use_when: Running weekly team meetings, launch standups, or a quarterly retrospective on how the team operates.

cards.title: Apply the ten team-building practices, including review mechanisms
cards.summary: Use the source's ten practices to set up a team so it does not become 'flavour of the month'.
cards.use_when: Designing how a new or reset team will operate over its first quarter — including its review cadence.

cards.title: Separate task roles from process roles and staff both
cards.summary: Assign explicit task and process roles so the group both achieves its aims and stays focused and harmonious.
cards.use_when: Fixing a team that hits tasks but has low morale, or one that is pleasant but never ships.

cards.title: Use Belbin team roles to balance a team, not to label people
cards.summary: Use the nine Belbin behavior clusters with their strengths and allowable weaknesses to adjust composition to the situation.
cards.use_when: Composing a pod or diagnosing why a capable group underdelivers — for example a team with strong execution but no external exploration.

cards.title: Play the Coordinator role without competing with the leader
cards.summary: Coordinate by identifying skills, giving feedback, smoothing disagreement and involving others in decisions — while avoiding power struggles.
cards.use_when: When a strong operator is placed in a junior or peer position on a project (e.g., a senior buyer on a cross-functional launch squad).

cards.title: Give a team drive with the Shaper role
cards.summary: Use Shaper behaviors — objectives, priorities, directive summaries — to break a drifting team out of inertia, with the source's tact caveats.
cards.use_when: When a project drifts and meetings end without decided priorities (campaign calendar, launch scope, backlog grooming).

cards.title: Recognize the failure signs of a poorly functioning team
cards.summary: Track the source's five early symptoms — resource resentment, cost overruns, slipped schedules, unclear responsibilities, diverted attention — as operational warning signals.
cards.use_when: Weekly or monthly team health check during a busy season, a launch, or peak fulfillment.

cards.title: Run team-building workshops across the interpersonal skill stack
cards.summary: Structure an offsite or workshop around self-management, role clarity, empathy, listening, and consensus building rather than generic activities.
cards.use_when: Planning a team offsite or reset day when the team ships but collaboration is strained.

cards.title: Team Role Gap Analysis: Which Roles Your Team Is Missing
cards.summary: Use Belbin's nine team roles and the essential/contributing split to diagnose which functions your team lacks before assigning work or hiring.
cards.use_when: Assessing an existing ecommerce team (buyer/merchandiser, marketer, ops, CX) or planning a hire, to check whether key functions are unstaffed before adding another person of the same type.

cards.title: Team Role Strengths and the Behaviours to Avoid
cards.summary: Each Belbin role has a characteristic strength and a matching failure mode; name both so a strength is not pushed into a liability.
cards.use_when: Running a team retrospective or 1:1 with a merchandiser, marketer or ops lead whose strength has started causing friction.

cards.title: Match Team Roles to Task Stage
cards.summary: Different roles matter at different stages of a project, so rotate who leads as work moves from direction to follow-through.
cards.use_when: Planning an ecommerce project such as a new category launch, site replatform or Q4 campaign, to decide who leads each phase.

cards.title: Communications Norms by Work Type: Routine/Emerging × Autonomous/Interdependent
cards.summary: Choose communication volume, direction and media based on whether work is routine or emerging and autonomous or interdependent.
cards.use_when: Setting comms norms for a distributed or multi-site ecommerce operation (buyers, warehouse, marketing, CX) or when reporting overhead is crowding out work.

cards.title: Shift the Leader Role by Quadrant: Defender, Manager, Lookout, Facilitator
cards.summary: A team leader's job changes by work quadrant — buffering, coordinating, scanning or facilitating.
cards.use_when: Setting a team lead's priorities for the week across routine operations and emerging channel challenges; diagnosing constant firefighting.

cards.title: Building Trust So People Take Commercial Risks
cards.summary: Trust is defined as safety to try and fail; it is earned slowly and lost instantly, and is a precondition for experimentation.
cards.use_when: Trying to get a team to run more tests, speak up about errors, or surface bad news early without blame.

cards.title: Choose a Conflict Mode Deliberately
cards.summary: Five conflict modes — and the situational conditions where each is appropriate.
cards.use_when: Handling a dispute over promotion timing, budget between channels, or an interdepartmental turf issue in an ecommerce operation.

cards.title: Tell Constructive Conflict from Destructive Conflict
cards.summary: Diagnose whether a dispute is clarifying issues or dividing the team, using the source's lists of effects.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to intervene in an ongoing conflict between merchandising and marketing, or between ops and customer service.

cards.title: Resolve Conflicts by Process Consultation, Not Verdict
cards.summary: Involve the conflicted member in defining the problem and shaping the solution so they become independent of the team's opinion.
cards.use_when: A buyer and a planner, or a store manager and a marketer, keep clashing and the manager is being asked to arbitrate every time.

cards.title: Pick a Leadership Style from Information and Time
cards.summary: Choose authoritarian, participative or delegative based on who holds the information, time pressure, and the team's capability.
cards.use_when: Deciding how to run a pricing decision, an incident response, or a creative brief in an ecommerce team.

cards.title: Free a Dominated Meeting: Leader Steps Out
cards.summary: Meetings can run without the leader present, which can increase candour and ownership.
cards.use_when: Recurring planning or retrospective meetings where your presence suppresses honest discussion or decisions stall awaiting approval.

cards.title: Measure Team Effectiveness Instead of Only Output
cards.summary: Use the source's assess-culture, vibrancy, meeting and behaviour measures to track the human side of execution.
cards.use_when: Quarterly health check on a store team before assuming that poor execution is a skill or process problem.

cards.title: Run Open Communication: 360 Feedback and Shared News
cards.summary: Institutionalize feedback and information flow so non-managers stop feeling uninformed.
cards.use_when: Diagnosing why ideas die between teams or why junior store staff say they hear about changes last.

cards.title: Leaders Should Set High Expectations and Model the Vision
cards.summary: A synthesized set of leader behaviours associated with outstanding leadership, to check against your own practice.
cards.use_when: Preparing for a team reset, a new category or channel push, or reviewing whether your leadership style supports strategy execution.

cards.title: Agree Norms and Start Before Full Consensus
cards.summary: Norms create a context for airing grievances; teams should proceed on agreed points and resolve disagreement as they go.
cards.use_when: Team forming or resetting after a reorg, when decisions are stalled waiting for everyone to agree.

cards.title: Diagnose the Growth Bottleneck: Traffic/Match vs. Conversion
cards.summary: Separate a low conversion rate into its two causes, wrong traffic or weak offer, before investing in CRO.
cards.use_when: Your store's conversion rate looks low relative to category norms and you are deciding whether to invest in CRO, new creative, or audience targeting.

cards.title: Identify the Owner's Core Skill to Locate the Missing Function
cards.summary: Name whether you are product/brand-led or media-buying-led to find which capability the business lacks.
cards.use_when: You are a founder stuck at a revenue plateau and deciding what to hire, learn, or outsource next.

cards.title: Use Equity and Non-Cash Levers to Land a Star Media Buyer
cards.summary: When margins are thin, compensate elite acquisition talent with equity or other levers instead of only cash salary.
cards.use_when: Your store is profitable but margins are too thin to pay a top-tier media buyer a full market salary, and you need that capability to scale.

cards.title: Why Ecommerce Can Scale Fast, and Where the Cash Trap Appears
cards.summary: Ecommerce revenue can scale quickly with the right acquisition person, but growth creates a cash-flow strain to plan for.
cards.use_when: You are forecasting an aggressive growth push (e.g., doubling revenue) and evaluating whether your cash can support it.

cards.title: Assess a sourcing advantage before treating it as an ecommerce moat
cards.summary: A strong sourcing eye for under/over-valued inventory is a core asset that partially substitutes for brand strength.
cards.use_when: You are assessing what actually differentiates your store and deciding how much to lean on sourcing versus acquisition spend.

cards.title: Sequence Brand Building After Revenue Growth
cards.summary: Prioritize near-term sales and revenue before investing in becoming a recognized brand, per the source's ordering.
cards.use_when: You are allocating effort between brand-building activities (content, identity, PR) and direct revenue-driving acquisition.

cards.title: Build the Team Around Proven Strength, Not Assumed Skill
cards.summary: Recognize which function you genuinely own and hire specifically for the gap, not for general 'management'.
cards.use_when: You are planning a headcount addition and unsure which role to prioritize for your next growth phase.

cards.title: Prioritize the Actual Bottleneck Over the Assumed One
cards.summary: When stuck at a plateau, verify whether your constraint is leads/traffic, conversion, or something else before acting.
cards.use_when: Your store has plateaued and you are deciding whether to fix traffic, conversion, or a different function.

cards.title: Assign cross-functional store ownership before choosing the first hire
cards.summary: The administrator owns contracts, partnerships, strategy, reporting and brand image, and a founder can fill this seat alone until revenue supports a hire.
cards.use_when: Deciding who your first operational hire should be when launching a new store or formalising an unstructured one-person operation.

cards.title: Staff customer service to clear purchase hesitation
cards.summary: Confused shoppers do not buy, so a customer service function should exist to answer questions and remove friction right before checkout.
cards.use_when: Designing your pre-purchase support coverage, chat/email staffing or FAQ operation to raise PDP and cart conversion.

cards.title: Keep emotional engagement alive through fulfillment and packaging
cards.summary: Because people buy emotionally, fulfillment should protect that feeling with tracking codes, receipts and packaging worth the wait.
cards.use_when: Setting fulfillment team responsibilities and post-purchase experience standards, including packaging, tracking and delivery communication.

cards.title: Build a digital marketing team that encodes your brand values
cards.summary: Marketing hires should understand company objectives and ethics, because buyers respond to brands whose values they can relate to.
cards.use_when: Writing the job spec for a media buyer or copywriter, or briefing campaign creative so ad messaging reflects the brand's actual positioning.

cards.title: Treat the website as a leaky bucket and staff developers to plug drop-off
cards.summary: Every step of the site leaks leads and the developer/designer role exists to fix those leaks by simplifying navigation and checkout.
cards.use_when: Diagnosing drop-off on product pages and in the checkout flow, or justifying a web development or design hire.

cards.title: Sequence the five ecommerce roles before launch
cards.summary: A workable store needs five functional silos — administrator, customer service, fulfillment, digital marketing, and web development/design — and a founder can cover several at low budget.
cards.use_when: Planning your first hires or deciding which functions a small store can safely leave with the founder.

cards.title: Screen candidates for drive, not just ability
cards.summary: A capable ecommerce team needs people who want to push to the next level, because you cannot get results from a bad team.
cards.use_when: Interviewing VAs, media buyers, operators or copywriters, or deciding whether a struggling team needs new people versus better process.

cards.title: The 2X Multiplier Effect: diagnose how much capability your team is actually giving you
cards.summary: Wiseman's core finding that leaders who amplify others get ~2x the capability from their people, and how to measure the gap on your own team.
cards.use_when: When you suspect your ecommerce team (merchandising, creative, supply chain, support) is underperforming relative to headcount and you are considering whether to hire more people or extract more from the people you have.

cards.title: Logic of addition vs. logic of multiplication: how to answer a growth target when headcount is frozen
cards.summary: Two competing budget logics - adding resources versus better leveraging existing ones - and how to reframe a growth target around capability rather than headcount.
cards.use_when: When you are asked to hit a revenue, launch, or margin target without additional budget or staff - a common ecommerce situation when paid acquisition costs rise or a peak season requires more output from the same team.

cards.title: Foundational assumption audit: fixed-scarcity vs. growth view of your team
cards.summary: The mindset difference that drives every management behavior - whether you treat intelligence as rare and fixed or as abundant and developable - and how to test your own assumptions.
cards.use_when: When making hiring, delegation, or promotion decisions for an ecommerce function (e.g. deciding whether a junior merchandiser or support agent can own a category, test plan, or supplier relationship), or when you notice you keep doing the thinking for the team.

cards.title: Talent Magnet vs. Empire Builder: deploy the best person even when you don't own them
cards.summary: Attract and deploy talent based on highest contribution rather than ownership, in contrast to hoarding resources and dividing people into 'mine' and 'not mine'.
cards.use_when: When staffing a high-stakes ecommerce initiative (site replatform, peak-season plan, new category launch) and you are choosing between holding your best people close versus lending them to where they will have the most impact.

cards.title: Liberator vs. Tyrant: create an environment that is both safe and intense
cards.summary: How to remove fear of judgment while keeping pressure high enough to demand people's best thinking, contrasted with a tense environment that suppresses capability.
cards.use_when: When running a team meeting, creative review, or post-mortem where you need honest input on pricing, creative, or a failed launch and you suspect people are self-censoring.

cards.title: Challenger vs. Know-It-All: set direction by seeding an opportunity instead of giving directives
cards.summary: How to frame a stretching opportunity and build belief it can be done, rather than issuing directives that showcase your own knowledge.
cards.use_when: When assigning a growth target to an ecommerce team - entering a new category, hitting a marketplace or subscription revenue goal, or improving a conversion rate - and you are tempted to hand over the answer.

cards.title: Debate Maker vs. Decision Maker: debate up front so execution doesn't stall
cards.summary: Drive decisions through rigorous debate before committing, so the broader team understands and executes instead of relitigating the decision afterwards.
cards.use_when: When making a consequential store decision - repricing a product line, killing a channel, restructuring a bundle, or changing a fulfillment vendor - especially when you would otherwise decide in a small inner circle.

cards.title: The Investor: give 51% of the vote and hand back the pen
cards.summary: Two delegation tactics - majority ownership of a decision (the leader keeps 49% as a consultant) and explicitly returning ownership after coaching - to build accountability without creating dependency.
cards.use_when: When delegating an ecommerce responsibility such as owning a category P&L, running a conversion test program, selecting a supplier, or managing a subscription retention roadmap.

cards.title: Coach a struggling store operator through questions and rehearsal
cards.summary: Use a calmer coaching style to test whether supervision is obstructing an otherwise capable ecommerce operator.
cards.use_when: When supervising a hands-on ecommerce process - buyer negotiations, ad-account management, live ops during peak - where an individual's performance is visibly dropping under your direct supervision.

cards.title: Working the extremes: develop leadership by fixing one weakness and topping off one strength
cards.summary: Rather than pursuing all-round excellence, focus development on neutralizing a single major weakness while extending one major strength.
cards.use_when: When planning your own development as an ecommerce operator moving into management, or when coaching a team lead through a performance plan with limited time and attention.

cards.title: The five disciplines as a diagnostic checklist for store leadership
cards.summary: A compact self-assessment pairing each Multiplier discipline with its Diminisher opposite, usable as a review checklist for an ecommerce manager.
cards.use_when: When auditing your own management behavior before a quarterly review, or when diagnosing why an underperforming ecommerce team is not delivering (merchandising, retention, or operations).

cards.title: Extract or suppress: measure how much of your team's intelligence you are actually accessing
cards.summary: Wiseman's argument that the leadership constraint is access to existing intelligence, not the supply of talented people, with concrete evidence from two managers in the same role.
cards.use_when: When deciding whether an ecommerce capability gap is a headcount problem or a management problem - for example, when a competent team delivers mediocre results on pricing, assortment, or experimentation.

cards.title: Talent Magnets vs Empire Builders: Diagnose Your Hiring and Team-Building Pattern
cards.summary: Contrasts leaders who attract and grow talent with those who hoard it as visible resources, and gives a self-diagnostic for team managers.
cards.use_when: Auditing how you build and staff your ecommerce team (category managers, buyers, creative, CX) and deciding whether you are developing people or just accumulating headcount.

cards.title: Look for Talent Everywhere: Widen Sourcing Beyond the Org Chart
cards.summary: Multipliers source capability across functions, geographies and boundaries rather than waiting for officially owned headcount.
cards.use_when: Filling a capability gap in an ecommerce business — e.g. paid social, feed management, CRO, PDP copy, fulfillment ops — when your own team lacks it.

cards.title: Identify and Label Native Genius: Effortless, Unconditional Strengths
cards.summary: Native genius is what someone does easily and freely, which is different from a strength rated on a 360 — find it by observation, then name it.
cards.use_when: Placing ecommerce staff — e.g. deciding whether a CX rep should stay on tickets or move into retention, lifecycle, or product work.

cards.title: Utilize People at Their Highest Point of Contribution
cards.summary: Move people from competent-but-narrow roles to roles matched to their discovered genius, then keep re-evaluating the ceiling.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to promote, transfer or re-scope a high-performing ecommerce employee — e.g. a strong CX rep, a strong buyer, a strong ad buyer.

cards.title: Shine a Specific, Public Spotlight on Contribution
cards.summary: Assign roles by strengths, tell each person why they were chosen, and make praise specific and visible so people connect their work to the outcome.
cards.use_when: Running an ecommerce team or agency pod — merch sprints, campaign launches, peak-season prep — where you want discretionary effort and less churn.

cards.title: Remove the Blockers — Including Prima Donnas You Cannot Afford to Lose
cards.summary: Talent growth requires removing people who consume the resources or tolerance that others need; this may mean exiting a high performer.
cards.use_when: Dealing with a talented but non-collaborative ecommerce player — a merchandiser, developer or buyer whose behavior is blocking team velocity.

cards.title: Get Out of the Way: Signal That Judgment Beats Placating the Boss
cards.summary: Leaders who explicitly authorize their teams to ignore them when needed unlock faster decisions.
cards.use_when: Running ecommerce operations where speed matters more than deference — pricing changes, campaign adjustments, inventory decisions, site fixes.

cards.title: Fast-First Hiring with Deep Finalist Diligence
cards.summary: Spend minutes eliminating clear mismatches and hours on the one or two candidates who fit, rather than uniform interview time.
cards.use_when: Screening a high volume of candidates for an ecommerce role where culture fit and specific capability both matter — e.g. buyers, performance marketers, warehouse leads.

cards.title: Loosely Defined Roles: Let Talent Flow to Where the Energy Is
cards.summary: Build roles around people's interests and capabilities, not fixed org-chart boxes, and let bottom-up proposals with broad support get funded.
cards.use_when: Scaling an ecommerce team where needs shift fast (new channel, new marketplace, new retention program) and rigid job descriptions slow you down.

cards.title: Humor as a Leadership Tool to Lower Defensiveness
cards.summary: Self-deprecating humor correlates with multiplier behavior because it removes the need to defend personal intelligence.
cards.use_when: Leading through high-pressure ecommerce moments — peak trading, a failed launch, a bad margin quarter — where tension is suppressing people's input.

cards.title: Spot Yourself as an Accidental Diminisher
cards.summary: Most diminishing behavior comes from inherited habits and past praise for personal intelligence rather than intent.
cards.use_when: Reviewing your own management behavior after noticing disengagement, low initiative or slow decisions in your ecommerce team.

cards.title: Diagnose a Vicious Talent Cycle Before It Becomes an Elephant Graveyard
cards.summary: Empire builders can attract strong people initially, then underuse them until they stagnate and stop leaving.
cards.use_when: Evaluating whether a team or department in your ecommerce business has quietly become a place where good people go stale.

cards.title: Don't Staff for Visible Headcount: The Hood Ornament Problem
cards.summary: Talent recruited for display rather than utilization becomes disenchanted and departs or disengages.
cards.use_when: Approving ecommerce headcount requests and deciding whether a new hire has a real mandate or only a title.

cards.title: Talent Magnet vs. Empire Builder: deploying talent instead of hoarding it
cards.summary: Distinguish leaders who acquire talent for status from those who deploy it at its highest point of contribution, and audit which pattern your team operates under.
cards.use_when: Assessing or redesigning how your ecommerce team's people are assigned to work (merchandising, buying, CRM, fulfillment), especially when headcount is growing but output is not.

cards.title: Genius watching: find native capability in your team and give it a role
cards.summary: A three-step method to identify what each person does easily and freely, test the hypothesis, then deploy that capability in real ecommerce work.
cards.use_when: Deciding who on your store team should own a new initiative, or when a role feels mismatched to the person in it.

cards.title: Pulling weeds: removing a destructive high performer from a store team
cards.summary: The arithmetic the authors use for removing a diminishing team member, and how to communicate the removal so the rest of the team can think again.
cards.use_when: A high-output but toxic person is dragging down a merchandising, buying or marketing pod and you keep postponing the decision.

cards.title: Tense versus intense: building a climate that surfaces real store problems
cards.summary: Distinguish climates that suppress information from those that demand focus, so problems with stock, forecasts or campaigns surface while they are still fixable.
cards.use_when: You need honest reporting on inventory, sell-through, forecast accuracy, ad performance or fulfillment issues and suspect people are watering down what they bring you.

cards.title: Liberator practice 1: create space by restraining yourself
cards.summary: Concrete restraint behaviors — holding back opinions, listening most of the time, operating consistently — that leave room for your team to contribute to store decisions.
cards.use_when: Leading a meeting on pricing, assortment, creative or site roadmap where your stated opinion would end discussion.

cards.title: Liberator practice 2: demand people's best work without demanding uncontrollable outcomes
cards.summary: Separate accountability for effort and execution from accountability for results the team cannot control — critical for marketplace, ad and conversion outcomes.
cards.use_when: Setting targets for ad spend, conversion rate, marketplace ranking or campaign performance where external factors move the number.

cards.title: Liberator practice 3: run rapid learning cycles around mistakes
cards.summary: Admit your own mistakes publicly and require fast learning rather than repetition, so testing velocity on the store stays high.
cards.use_when: After a failed campaign, a mispriced promotion, an out-of-stock event or a losing landing-page test.

cards.title: Talent Magnets create a recruiting flywheel by letting people leave well
cards.summary: Treat internal mobility and alumni as recruiting assets rather than losses, to keep a pipeline of strong ecommerce operators.
cards.use_when: A strong team member is leaving for an internal role elsewhere or another company, and you decide how to respond.

cards.title: Audit the hierarchy's built-in drag on idea flow
cards.summary: Hierarchy itself tilts the playing field; the same person can become an accidental diminisher just by moving up, so audit your own casual remarks.
cards.use_when: Reviewing why good ideas stop reaching you from merchandising, customer service, fulfillment or agency teams.

cards.title: Improve learning capacity by pairing the right people with learning-oriented work
cards.summary: The book's framing that the multiplier effect depends less on raw leadership intelligence than on being 'smart enough to learn' — applied to how you staff store initiatives.
cards.use_when: Building or reshuffling a store team for a new channel, marketplace or retention program where the playbook is not yet known.

cards.title: Build an intense, not tense, team environment
cards.summary: Distinguish intense climates that demand best thinking from tense climates that suppress it, and use that to run your ecommerce team.
cards.use_when: Operational team management: setting the tone in weekly standups, planning sessions, or cross-functional meetings (merchandising, acquisition, fulfillment) — and diagnosing why contributions are shallow.

cards.title: Use poker-chip talk budgets to free team space
cards.summary: Cap your own meeting airtime with a fixed number of 'chips' so others co-create the plan instead of reacting to yours.
cards.use_when: Leading a strategy session, planning meeting, or cross-functional review where you tend to dominate the discussion and ideas aren't surfacing.

cards.title: Label your opinions as soft or hard
cards.summary: Separate musings from decisions so casual comments don't become unintended policy pushing your team's only safe ideas.
cards.use_when: Any leadership communication where a throwaway comment risks being treated as a directive — team meetings, Slack, planning reviews, 1:1s.
